title: Tiered failover storylines for sales
body:
Purpose and audience: This note is for Sales and Solutions Engineering to use when positioning Redwood's reliability story to engineering and platform buyers. It focuses on tiered failover patterns (model substitution, capacity tiering, and multi-region fallbacks) and provides short customer-facing scripts, incident vignettes, competitive differentiators, and suggested objection responses. Use this as a living draft — pull short vignettes into deal-specific emails or slide decks.

Executive summary (one-liner): Redwood guarantees predictable behavior under stress by combining model-compatible fallbacks, capacity tiers, and automated region-aware routing, so your app stays useful and trustworthy even during partial outages.

Core principles to communicate (keeps the message consistent):
- Predictable degradation, not surprising failure: We aim to preserve end-user intent wherever possible instead of returning errors.
- Transparent controls: Customers set policies for cost vs. fidelity — e.g., prefer lower-cost quantized model versus added latency for the full model.
- Observable decisions: Every automatic fallback emits events and traces visible in the Console so you can audit what happened and why.
- Fail-safe fallbacks: We keep conservative defaults (e.g., degrade to short responses, prefer cached prefixes) and provide higher-fidelity options under contract.

Three-tier failover storyline (for concise sales pitch):
1) Level 1 — graceful local measures (0–100ms impact): prefix caching, KV reuse, and request coalescing. Your app stays snappy, typically no visible change.
2) Level 2 — service-aware model fallbacks (100–500ms): switch from full-precision model to a compatible quantized variant or smaller family model. Slight change in style/length, same API surface.
3) Level 3 — capacity or regional fallback (500ms+): route to another region or burst capacity tier with clear SLAs; if unavailable, apply summarized responses to guarantee continuity.

Customer-facing scripts (bite-sized, pick one depending on audience):
- For platform engineers: “If the primary model or pool hits capacity, Redwood automatically routes traffic to a vetted fallback model that preserves API shape and response semantics. You get traces of every decision and can tune policies per-route.”
- For product managers: “We prioritize user intent — during incidents we return condensed, actionable responses instead of failures so your product remains useful while the backend recovers.”
- For exec/legal reviewers: “We define measurable continuity objectives (time-to-degrade, max-quality-loss) and can provide contractual language around fallbacks and region failover behavior.”

Incident vignettes (usable in slides or emails):
- Latency storm, web traffic spike: Primary pool saturation; Redwood applied Level 1 and Level 2 measures within seconds. End users saw a 10–15% reduction in token length; no errors. Business impact: zero visible downtime, 2% drop in average revenue-per-session.
- Regional outage (cloud provider AZ down): Automated region-aware routing shifted 40% of critical queries to secondary region and the rest to quantized variants. Engineers had full decision logs and rolled back policy in 12 minutes. Business impact: degraded but continuous experience for customers.
- Model regression during rollout: Canary detected quality drift; automatic fallback to previous version plus throttled canary traffic until rollback was approved. This prevented a visible spike in bad responses to customers.

Competitive angles and how to use them (short bullets):
- Against generic managed endpoint providers: They often expose raw failure modes (403/500). Sell Redwood as the platform that transforms failures into controlled degradation with auditable decisions.
- Against single-region self-hosted frameworks: Emphasize Redwood’s multi-region routing + capacity tiers built into the control plane; customers get enterprise continuity without custom ops glue.
- Against low-cost inference vendors: Cost plays a role, but highlight our quality-preserving fallbacks (model compatibility, curated smaller models) vs. simplistic throttling that just drops requests.

Objection handling (common pushbacks):
- “I don’t want model outputs to change unpredictably.” Response: "Fallbacks are predictable and configurable. You can pin per-route policies, lock fallback model versions, and receive pre-approved sample outputs for compliance-sensitive flows"
- “We need audited proof for regulators.” Response: "Every fallback decision emits logs and signed events that integrate with your SIEM and audit pipeline. We also support KMS-backed signing for private deployments"
- “Will routing to another region increase latency too much?” Response: "We expose latency/cost tradeoffs per-failover path and can apply client-side hedging or local cache-first policies to mitigate user-facing latency"

Suggested slide deck snippets (3–4 bullets each):
- Slide: How we avoid downtime: quick bullets — automated fallbacks, multi-region routing, canary quality checks, audit trails.
- Slide: What the user sees: no errors, slightly shorter responses, or temporarily simplified results — never 500s.
- Slide: Controls for your team: per-route policy editor, rollback playbooks, and monthly reports on fallbacks and quality drift.

Language and tone tips for reps:
- Avoid engineering jargon for execs — use words like "continuity" and "intent preservation."
- For infra teams, use concrete SLO/behavior numbers (e.g., "99.9% of spiky load handled by local caching and quantized fallbacks").
- Emphasize observability: customers love being able to replay decisions for root cause.

Operational checklist to attach to deals (one-liner items):
- Define continuity objectives (max permissible quality loss).
- Decide default fallback models and pin rules.
- Configure alert thresholds for failover events.
- Establish audit export destination (S3/Cloud logging).
- Run a simulated failover as part of onboarding.

Example email template to send to buyers after a demo (short):
Subject: follow-up — continuity and failover plan
Hi <Name>,
Thanks for the demo today. As discussed, Redwood uses tiered fallbacks (cache -> compatible-quantized-model -> region/burst) to keep your feature usable during incidents. Attached is the proposed continuity objective doc and a sample policy for your critical routes. Happy to set up a runbook review with your SREs next week.
Best,
Nina

Next steps for this doc (team action items):
- UX: extract 2–3 one-liners for the sales cheat sheet (owner: Sofia).
- Solutions Eng: add a short demo script showing a simulated canary regression (owner: Miguel).
- Legal: draft fallback contract language for enterprise (owner: Ravi).

Notes and open questions:
- Need guidance on how to quantify "quality loss" for short answers in SLAs — product/research alignment required.
- If customers want deterministic output in fallbacks, we should document sampling/temperature defaults and exportability of fallback samples.

End of note.

This doc is intentionally concise and modular. Pull sections for deal collateral — the goal is to make reliability tangible and defensible in customer conversations.
